cf.title: Progress reporting: a debug trace and a test framework

input.subject: Progress reporting: a debug trace and a test framework

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: ten progress fixes this year and a live bug in WaitForOlderSnapshots() show the area needs tests. The surviving objections are fixable design points at level 2. maintenance-fit-1 and already-exists-1 ask where the checks would run, since default builds skip most of test_progress. maintenance-fit-2 asks how much of the test is tied to execution order. No level fails outright, but only the author has spoken in the visible thread.

brief.title: Progress reporting debug trace and test_progress test module
brief.problem: Progress reporting is tested only by sampling pg_stat_progress_* views at one moment, which needs concurrency or injection points and misses the succession of values a command reports. Bugs in progress values and undocumented phases or parameters go unnoticed. The audience is Postgres developers and the regression suite.
brief.proposed_design: A compile-time macro PROGRESS_DEBUG, plus a developer GUC trace_progress, logs every progress state change at LOG_SERVER_ONLY from backend_progress.c. A new TAP module test_progress replays each backend's trace and checks general rules and per-command phase and value sequences. A second test checks that reported phases appear in system_views.sql and monitoring.sgml.
user_visible_surface: Developer GUC trace_progress, modeled on trace_syncscan, present only in PROGRESS_DEBUG builds.
Server log lines "progress start/update/end: <command> relid=... idx:old->new" when the trace is on.
New test module src/test/modules/test_progress with ProgressCheck.pm and DocPhases.pm.
author_claims: Without PROGRESS_DEBUG the object code has the same instruction stream as master, and meson test time differs within noise (84.9 s against 84.2 s).
With the option, meson test takes about 7 s more and check-world logs grow from about 70 MB to 135 MB, all from test_progress's own trace.
Reverting this year's ten progress fixes one at a time, v6 catches nine; five of the checks were written knowing those fixes.
Of 301 held-out blind mutants of progress calls, test_progress catches 285 (94.7%); today's tests catch 10 of a 150-mutant sample.
The trace found a live bug: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY shows lockers_done 2 with lockers_total 1, because WaitForOlderSnapshots() does not reset PROGRESS_WAITFOR_* values.
brief.thread_state: Only the author's two messages are visible. He mentions that Michael suggested a separate thread and that Álvaro thought a compile option was enough, but no replies from others appear.
unclear: Whether any buildfarm animal or cfbot would define PROGRESS_DEBUG; without one, most of test_progress always skips.
How ProgressCheck.pm's per-parameter descriptions are kept up to date, and who must edit them when a command's progress reporting changes.
Whether the known-accepted blips in @ACCEPTED and the WaitForOlderSnapshots() bug get separate fixes, and in which patch.
How the trace behaves inside critical sections in v6; v5 said the line is built on the stack, v6 does not repeat this.
Whether the trace output format is meant to stay stable for other tools.

objections.title: Most checks run only on builds that define PROGRESS_DEBUG
objections.failure_scenario: A committer changes the phases of VACUUM or REPACK and runs cfbot and the buildfarm, and everything passes because test_progress skips there. The expected sequences in ProgressCheck.pm go stale. The next developer who builds with PROGRESS_DEBUG finds failures that someone else's commit caused, possibly months later.
objections.argument: The commit message says that without PROGRESS_DEBUG only the progress.h description check runs, and measurements.txt shows test_progress taking 0.36 s on default builds. No part of the proposal names a buildfarm animal or cfbot task that defines the macro. A check that fails only on builds nobody routinely runs does not warn the person who broke it. The author keeps the compile option because of Álvaro's view in message #2, but trace_progress already keeps the trace out of other tests' logs.
objections.author_must_show: Which cfbot task or buildfarm animal will build with PROGRESS_DEBUG, or why can the code not always be compiled in and gated by trace_progress alone?

critic.reasoning: The commit message says the rest of the test is skipped without PROGRESS_DEBUG, and neither message names a cfbot task or buildfarm animal that defines it. Following trace_syncscan explains the macro but does not say where the checks run.

objections.title: New compile macro and GUC where injection points could carry the trace
objections.failure_scenario: No buildfarm animal or cfbot task defines PROGRESS_DEBUG, so on every build in the cycle test_progress runs only the progress.h description check and skips the rest. A later patch breaks a phase sequence, and nobody finds out until someone builds with the macro by hand.
objections.argument: Postgres already has a build option for test-only hooks in backend code: --enable-injection-points, and cfbot and some buildfarm animals already use it. An injection point in backend_progress.c, with a callback in the test module that logs the backend's progress state, would give the same trace without a new macro in pg_config_manual.h or a new GUC. Message #1 and the commit message name injection points only as a way to sample the views at one moment, not as a way to carry the trace. Following trace_syncscan is existing practice, but that practice is rarely compiled in.
objections.author_must_show: Why can an injection point in backend_progress.c, with a callback in test_progress, not produce the same trace on builds that already enable injection points?

critic.reasoning: The thread mentions injection points only for sampling the views, and does not say why one in backend_progress.c could not carry the trace. Copying trace_syncscan lowers the weight, but the question stands because cfbot already builds with injection points.

objections.title: Exact per-command sequences make every progress change edit the test module
objections.failure_scenario: A patch adds a VACUUM index cycle or reorders a REPACK step and changes no progress semantics. 001_progress.pl then fails on the exact phase succession or on a value checked per parameter. The patch author must learn and edit a large Perl replay module that no committer in the visible thread has said they will look after.
objections.argument: v6-0001 is 118 KB, and its commit message says the test checks the succession of phases and an expected value for every parameter of every command, with failure variants, parallel builds, autovacuum and failsafe. This couples test expectations to the internal order of execution of many commands, beyond the documented contract. Only the author's messages appear. Michael and Álvaro are mentioned in message #2 but have not replied, so no qualified committer has taken on the aftermath. The @ACCEPTED list also needs someone to keep it current.
objections.author_must_show: Which checks follow from documented progress semantics and which from current execution order, and which committer has agreed to keep ProgressCheck.pm current when commands change?

critic.reasoning: The commit message confirms exact phase successions and a value per parameter for every command, so changes to execution order will need edits in ProgressCheck.pm. The missing committer owner belongs under committability and should not add weight to the verdict.

refuted.title: Most checks run only in builds nobody is shown to make
refuted.failure_scenario: A patch in 2027 breaks a REPACK progress counter. cfbot and the buildfarm build without PROGRESS_DEBUG, so test_progress runs only the progress.h description check and passes. The bug ships, and the mutation results never apply in practice.
refuted.argument: The 94.7% catch rate in measurements.txt was measured on a -DPROGRESS_DEBUG build. Neither message names a buildfarm animal, a cfbot task or a CI setting that would define the macro. In message #2 the author keeps the compile option because Álvaro preferred it, but nothing says who turns it on. A developer tool that only its author runs gives the tree little beyond a one-time bug sweep.
refuted.author_must_show: Which buildfarm animals or cfbot tasks will build with PROGRESS_DEBUG, and has anyone who runs them agreed?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which states the same gap and also names the alternative of gating by trace_progress alone.

refuted.title: Every progress patch must update ProgressCheck.pm, for a few users
refuted.failure_scenario: A contributor adds a phase or a parameter to commands/progress.h. The description check runs on every build and fails until they edit a Perl description, and a per-command value expectation, in a module they have never seen. They pay this cost even if nobody runs the full trace checks.
refuted.argument: The commit message says a new or renumbered parameter "has to be described before the test passes", on any build. So the cost falls on everyone who touches progress reporting. The gain reaches only people who build with PROGRESS_DEBUG, and the first objection shows no such group is named. Message #1 shows the check firing on 1378aa13430, which points to real churn.
refuted.author_must_show: Who besides the author has agreed to keep ProgressCheck.pm's descriptions current, and would the description check be welcome by itself, without the trace?

critic.reasoning: The description check runs on any build, so its gain is not limited to PROGRESS_DEBUG builds; message #1 shows it flagging the undescribed parameter from 1378aa13430. The per-command value expectations are skipped on default builds; maintenance-fit-2 covers that cost.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the developer option trace_progress in guc_parameters.dat, present only in PROGRESS_DEBUG builds.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: ProgressCheck.pm holds a description of every progress parameter and exact phase sequences that each progress change must update.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch edits backend_progress.c and backend_status.c; the author reports an unchanged instruction stream without PROGRESS_DEBUG.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: A new compile macro carries the trace although injection points are an existing build option for test hooks.

questions: Which cfbot task or buildfarm animal will build with PROGRESS_DEBUG, and has its owner agreed?
Why can the trace code not always be compiled in and gated by trace_progress alone?
Why can an injection point in backend_progress.c, with a callback in test_progress, not produce the same trace on builds that already enable injection points?
Which checks in 001_progress.pl follow from documented progress semantics, and which only from the current order of execution?
How does the v6 trace build its log line when progress is reported inside a critical section?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows backend_progress.c and the TAP test infrastructure would have to own it. The author mentions Michael and Álvaro, but neither has posted in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a 118 KB test module whose per-command expectations need an edit whenever a command's progress reporting or execution order changes, for as long as the module exists. The owner also signs for the trace code in backend_progress.c, the @ACCEPTED list and the PROGRESS_DEBUG build staying green.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v6 four weeks after v5 with measurements, a mutation benchmark and a bug reproduction, and offered a follow-up patch for the counter resets.

priority.reason: The audience is Postgres developers who change progress reporting, and the trace has already found bugs on master. v6-0001 is 118 KB, mostly Perl expectations for many commands, and no committer has replied in the visible thread.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can check that the trace is safe inside critical sections or that default builds are unchanged beyond the author's object-code comparison. The share of ProgressCheck.pm that is tied to execution order is also not visible.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Report checkpoint progress with pg_stat_progress_checkpoint
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Michael Paquier, Andres Freund, Julien Rouhaud
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread started as a proposal to log checkpoint progress in the server log. After objections it became a pg_stat_progress_checkpoint view that reports the checkpoint phase, flags, start LSN, start time and per-phase counters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The final close came because the author stopped responding after Andres Freund marked the patch waiting on author for a docs build failure and noted that the architectural feedback had not reached a conclusion. Earlier, Michael Paquier returned it because the view was too complex and carried fields of little use, such as next_flags, start LSN and most flag values. Julien Rouhaud objected that the view showed the initial checkpoint flags instead of how the checkpoint was behaving now. Andres Freund measured progress-update overhead in BufferSync() on large shared_buffers.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: There has been no updates on this thread for some time, so this has been switched as Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Report checkpoint progress with pg_stat_progress_checkpoint
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_stat_progress_checkpoint view that reports the phase, flags, start LSN and other details of the running checkpoint or restartpoint. It started as a proposal to log checkpoint progress in the server log, but reviewers asked for a progress view instead.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with Feedback because the view needed simplification: several fields and flags were of little use for monitoring, and the phase names were too long. Andres Freund objected that the view definition makes pg_rewrite bigger, and he asked for proof that the progress counters do not slow down checkpoints with many dirty buffers. The last measurement shown, a manual checkpoint taking 2.457 s with the patch against 2.334 s without, got no reply.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think that what's proposed could be simplified, and we had better remove the fields that are not that useful.

precedents_retrieved.title: libpq trace log
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch began as a libpq client-side query log enabled by connection parameters or environment variables (logdir/PGLOGDIR, logsize/PGLOGSIZE). After review it was narrowed to reworking PQtrace() so it prints one line per protocol message with a timestamp, and enabling it without recompiling was deferred.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Earlier, David Steele moved the patch to PG13 because, in agreement with Andres, it was not clear where the patch was going. The last message before the decision is a review by Alvaro Herrera, who agreed with the one-line-per-message direction but asked for changes. He objected to a frontend_entry[MAXPGPATH] array in pg_conn and listed smaller fixes. The thread shows no new patch or author reply after that review before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This seems to make pg_conn much larger than we'd like.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_tracing
precedents_retrieved.summary: A contrib-style extension, pg_tracing, generates distributed-tracing spans for planner, executor and nested queries, using trace context passed in SQLCommenter comments or a sampling rate. Spans go into a shared memory buffer, and an external forwarder reads them with pg_tracing_consume_spans() and sends them to a trace collector.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas recommended that the author publish pg_tracing as a separate extension on GitHub, and Nikita Malakhov agreed. Heikki's own message is not shown; only the replies quote it. In March 2024 the author said he was moving pg_tracing to a GitHub repository, and the entry was later withdrawn. The visible messages do not show a technical objection that blocked the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: To give a quick update: following Heikki's suggestion, I'm currently working on getting pg_tracing as a separate extension on github.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add index scan progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds index vacuum progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum, with counts of indexes to process and indexes processed, including indexes handled by parallel vacuum workers. Later versions keep worker progress in a hash table in the main shared memory segment, so the progress views can read it after a worker exits.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Robert Haas objected to the use of the main shared memory segment and to the locking it adds to progress reporting, which is meant to be low overhead. They asked that workers pass data to the leader through the parallel vacuum's dynamic shared memory, and that the leader report it with the existing progress fields; Masahiko Sawada agreed. Greg Stark returned the patch because of these design changes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
That is, I am imagining that you would want to use DSM to propagate
data from workers back to the leader and then have the leader report
the data using the existing progress-reporting facilities.

precedents_retrieved.title: improve DEBUG1 logging of parallel workers for CREATE INDEX
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the DEBUG1 message for parallel CREATE INDEX to report parallel workers launched as well as planned. It later grew into a CREATE INDEX (VERBOSE) option, with matching REINDEX (VERBOSE) output, that reports parallel worker use at INFO level.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it after Michael Paquier pointed to Tom's view that such details should come from an extended EXPLAIN rather than VERBOSE options on more commands. Michael also asked how clients would consume the output. The author wrote that the best approach needs more discussion, and that fixing only the REINDEX DEBUG1 output did not make much sense.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm +-0 about the
VERBOSE option attached to more commands, as it is a bit harder for
clients to catch the information wanted.

precedents_retrieved.title: Enhance file_fdw to report processed and skipped tuples in COPY progress
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes file_fdw report tuples_processed and tuples_skipped (rows skipped with on_error = 'ignore') in pg_stat_progress_copy. file_fdw already reports some columns there, such as relid and bytes_processed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Masahiko Sawada noted that file_fdw's use of COPY progress does not work well, because one query can run several file_fdw scans at once and each backend has only one progress slot. The author first argued this was a separate, existing problem, then withdrew the patch: wider COPY progress support in file_fdw would make wrong progress reports more common.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don’t think the fact that the issue
already exists is a good reason to introduce more, and likely more common,
scenarios where it could occur.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add description about using geqo to EXPLAIN or debug log.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal adds a way for users to see whether the planner used GEQO for a query, so they can tune geqo_threshold without recompiling with GEQO_DEBUG. It started as a debug-level log message and became an EXPLAIN (geqo) option that prints a GeqoDetails line.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers agreed the information belongs in EXPLAIN but asked for changes to the output. David G. Johnston said one GEQO line is wrong because a query can have several join trees, and that the line should not repeat geqo_threshold. Jacob Champion questioned printing GeqoDetails when GEQO was not used. The visible messages show no revised patch after this review in July 2022, and the entry was returned with feedback in October.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The presentation of only a single geqo result seems incorrect given that multiple trees can exist.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. P1 and P2 add a checkpoint progress view and were returned for view complexity, unused fields and checkpoint overhead, none of which applies to a compiled-out trace and test module. Message #1 says the patches were first posted in another thread and moved here at Michael's suggestion, and message #2 reports that Álvaro thought a compile option was enough. The visible thread records no rejection reason from that earlier thread.

The proposal adds no SQL syntax, catalog object, dumped setting or psql change. The trace_progress developer option follows the existing TRACE_SYNCSCAN/trace_syncscan pattern and exists only in PROGRESS_DEBUG builds, so default builds and their users see no change. The listed files do not include config.sgml, so the option's entry under developer options is not shown. The proposal does not say whether the log line format is meant to stay stable for tools; both points are documentation details, not standards objections.

The proposal adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, replication or wire-protocol state. It is a compile-time trace and a developer GUC that write server log lines, plus a TAP module. Default builds keep the same instruction stream, so extension ABI is unchanged; logging inside critical sections in PROGRESS_DEBUG builds can only be checked in the code.

The trace is compiled in only with PROGRESS_DEBUG, a developer build option, and writes only relids and integer progress values to the server log at LOG_SERVER_ONLY, never to clients. Even if trace_progress were user-settable like trace_syncscan, the worst case is log growth on a debug build, and production builds are not affected.

Hot-path cost is not raised: the trace is compiled out by default, and measurements.txt shows the same instruction stream and test time within noise. The listed precedents concern a checkpoint progress view and do not apply.

The views and injection points only sample values at one moment, so they do not cover the full sequence of reports, and no extension can see progress writes. The objection above is about reusing an existing mechanism, and the need itself is real.

The problem itself is shown. Ten progress fixes this year, a live WaitForOlderSnapshots() bug, and current tests catching 10 of 150 mutants show the area needs testing. The open demand questions are who runs the PROGRESS_DEBUG build and who pays for maintaining the descriptions.
